extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in technology/media industry practices and journalism ethics (journalists, editors, media observers)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards implied by a reporting piece about how a news outlet uses AI for content production, disclosure, and monetization. Focuses on editorial transparency, attribution, accuracy, and the tradeoffs between SEO-driven revenue and journalistic standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear, prominent disclosure of AI-generated content
rubrics_metrics.description: Automated or AI-generated stories should be disclosed to readers in a clear, prominent way rather than buried or hidden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece notes that over 70 articles appeared with the byline “CNET Money Staff” since November, but "an editorial note about a robot generating those stories was only visible if readers did a little clicking around." Contrast with AP labeling some stories as automated with a footer — but the footer may still be unclear to readers. Anti-pattern: disclosures hidden behind extra clicks or obscure language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate author attribution and author-page consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Bylines should accurately reflect authorship and be properly linked to author pages showing the full scope of the author's work, bio, and headshot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: mortgage stories carry Justin Jaffe's byline but are not listed on his actual author page; instead they appear on a different author page that only contains his mortgage rate stories. This can mislead readers about who wrote what and whether content was human-authored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal transparency about AI tools and workflows
rubrics_metrics.description: Staff across the newsroom should know what AI tools are used, how they're used, and what the human workflow around them is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article reports that "few people at the outlet know specific details about the AI tools — or the human workflow around them" and that siloed teams made it difficult for journalists to understand the chain of command. Anti-pattern: teams unaware whether a colleague's byline corresponds to AI output or human writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human oversight to prevent harmful errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Automated content—especially on fields that can cause real-world harm (finance, cybersecurity, health)—must be reviewed to ensure accuracy and to avoid errors that "could cause direct harm to readers."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: an unnamed staffer reported unattributed AI-written content was sent to subscribers of a cybersecurity email newsletter and had errors that could harm readers. Guidance implies rigorous human fact-checking and editorial review before publication and distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit AI to appropriate, formulaic, high-volume tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Use AI primarily for repetitive, narrowly-structured reporting (e.g., mortgage rates, earnings reports) rather than for substantive investigative or interpretive journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece notes the Associated Press used Wordsmith for earnings reports and sports (high-volume/formulaic tasks) and that mortgage rate stories are "perfectly suited to being generated by AI." Guidance: reserve automation for tasks that free journalists for more thoughtful work; anti-pattern: using AI to replace substantive reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain to readers what 'automated' or 'using technology' means
rubrics_metrics.description: When labeling content as automated, provide an understandable explanation so readers know what technologies and processes were used and what implications that has for accuracy and oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The AP labels stories as automated with a footer noting the use of automated tools, but the article points out a reader "may not understand what it means that the story was created 'using technology.'" Guidance: disclosures should define the level of automation and human involvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid content farming purely for SEO/affiliate revenue at the expense of credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations should not prioritize publishing mass-produced, SEO-optimized content whose primary purpose is to drive affiliate fees over maintaining the outlet’s journalistic mission and credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Red Ventures' explicit business model is to rank highly in Google for 'high-intent' queries and monetize via affiliate links. The article documents topics like 'Can You Buy a Gift Card With a Credit Card?' as designed to rank and convert. Anti-pattern: flooding search algorithms with low-quality copy engineered only to extract affiliate payouts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain legal and regulatory compliance when automating specialized beats
rubrics_metrics.description: Automated content in regulated areas (finance, legal, health) must meet legal requirements and standards applicable to that subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The company justified tools as a way of "making sure that legal requirements for writing about finance are met." Guidance: automation should be used only with processes that ensure compliance and appropriate oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear editorial ownership and chain-of-command for AI decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be a documented chain of command indicating who decides to deploy AI tools, who oversees them, and who is accountable for resulting content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article highlights confusion around who at Red Ventures or CNET was responsible for AI practices and that a siloed structure made it hard for staff to know who was using what tools. Guidance: assign named roles and public points of contact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Named points of contact and accountability for AI practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations should designate identifiable spokespeople or contacts for questions about AI usage and disclosures, and respond transparently to inquiries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Red Ventures and its sites directed questions to specific executives (e.g., Lance Davis) and at times listed Davis as point of contact. The piece criticizes Red Ventures for refusing to answer questions about the tools it uses. Guidance: provide accessible contacts and transparent answers to media and staff queries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use automation to genuinely free journalists for more thoughtful work, not to justify staff cuts
rubrics_metrics.description: If automation is presented as a tool to free staff for higher-value journalism, the organization should actually enable that outcome rather than using it as cover for layoffs and reduced investment in reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article reports that while the tool was sold as a way to free up staff time, several staffers departed and morale dropped after layoffs and restructuring. Anti-pattern: automation touted as freeing staff while simultaneous layoffs and reduced editorial investment occur.
